title: Ethiopian Yellow Split Pea Alicha
community: All of Ethiopia — the mild yellow pea stew of the fasting platter
author: Mama Tigist
desc: Ethiopian Kik Alicha — yellow split peas simmered until completely soft in a golden sauce of onion, turmeric, garlic, and ginger without berbere. The mild, golden-yellow counterpart to Misir Wat on the fasting platter — gentle, creamy, and deeply nourishing.
longDesc: Kik Alicha is the mild partner to Misir Wat — the same position that Alicha Wat holds to Key Wat in the meat world. Yellow split peas cooked with turmeric and onion (no berbere) produce a golden, mild stew that provides balance on the fasting platter. Its gentle flavour makes it the most accessible Ethiopian dish for those new to the cuisine.
steps: Cook onion in oil until very golden — 10 minutes.
Add turmeric and ground ginger. Stir 1 minute.
Add garlic and fresh ginger. Cook 1 minute.
Add washed split peas. Stir to coat.
Add water. Bring to a boil.
Reduce heat. Simmer covered 40—45 minutes until completely soft.
Stir occasionally — peas will partially dissolve.
Season. The stew should be thick and golden.
chefTips: No berbere — the gentleness is the point.
The peas should be very soft — nearly dissolving.
Turmeric is generous here — the golden colour is important.
commonMistakes: Under-cooking — peas must be very soft.
cookingScience: Yellow split peas (dehulled and split yellow field peas) cook faster than whole peas because the hull has been removed — the cotyledons absorb water directly. The turmeric's curcumin dissolves into the oil, producing the characteristic golden colour throughout the stew.
sustainabilityTips: Split peas — one of the most water-efficient legumes.
servedWith: Alongside Misir Wat and Shiro on the fasting platter
culturalNote: Kik Alicha is the gentle welcome of Ethiopian fasting cuisine — the dish that even the most heat-sensitive guest can eat with joy. Its golden colour and mild flavour make the fasting platter complete by providing the essential contrast to the red berbere wats.
